title: US Stocks Post Modest October Gains as Bond Yields and Oil Keep Investors Cautious

author.name: Finance Desk
author.bio: The Finance Desk provides updates on U.S. equities, Treasury yields, and global commodity markets.

excerpt: U.S. stocks opened October with modest gains as Treasury yields eased from multi-year highs, while oil prices and inflation concerns kept markets volatile.
seoTitle: Wall Street Starts October Higher as Treasury Yields Retreat and Oil Remains Above $100
seoDescription: U.S. stocks opened October with modest gains as Treasury yields eased from multi-year highs, while oil prices and inflation concerns kept markets volatile.

content.text: U.S. stocks began the fourth quarter with modest gains on Thursday, October 1, as investors returned to equities after a difficult stretch in the bond market. The advance was limited, however, with Treasury yields remaining elevated and crude oil prices rising sharply. The session illustrated the competing forces currently shaping Wall Street: optimism around technology and artificial-intelligence investment is providing support for equities, while inflation concerns, expensive energy and high long-term borrowing costs continue to create volatility. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/dow-futures-hit-three-month-low-yields-surge-micron-earnings-offer-support-2026-10-01/))

The S&P 500 gained 0.20% to 7,666.48, ending a three-session losing streak. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 20.69 points, or 0.04%, to 50,926.74, while the Nasdaq Composite added 0.04% to 26,871.60. The Russell 2000, which tracks smaller companies, performed somewhat better, advancing 0.3%. The relatively small moves reflected a market that was still cautious despite recovering from an early selloff.

A major reason for the rebound was a reversal in Treasury yields during the session. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield initially moved to a 24-year high above 5.3%, adding pressure to stocks, before retreating later in the day. The decline in yields helped investors return to equities and supported the market's modest recovery from morning losses. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/dow-futures-hit-three-month-low-yields-surge-micron-earnings-offer-support-2026-10-01/))

The move in the bond market is particularly important because September ended with one of the sharpest quarterly increases in Treasury yields in decades. Reuters reported that the 10-year yield posted its largest quarterly rise since 1994. Higher yields raise financing costs across the U.S. economy and can also affect stock valuations by increasing the return investors can obtain from government bonds. The recent jump has consequently become one of the biggest macroeconomic concerns facing Wall Street as the fourth quarter begins. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/dow-futures-hit-three-month-low-yields-surge-micron-earnings-offer-support-2026-10-01/))

The bond-market pressure has not been caused by Federal Reserve policy alone. Investors are also responding to strong economic activity, persistent inflation pressures, rising energy costs and the amount of debt being supplied to the market. Longer-term yields can increase even when expectations for immediate Fed rate hikes decline, because investors may demand greater compensation for inflation, fiscal and duration risks. That distinction has become increasingly important during the latest market selloff.

Economic data released Thursday provided mixed signals. The Institute for Supply Management said its manufacturing purchasing managers index slipped only slightly to 54.5 in September from 54.6 in August. A reading above 50 indicates expansion, meaning U.S. factory activity continued to grow. New orders increased to 55.3 from 53.7, while order backlogs also rose, suggesting demand remains solid. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/us-manufacturing-steady-september-input-prices-increase-2026-10-01/))

At the same time, the manufacturing survey showed a substantial increase in price pressures. The ISM measure of prices paid for inputs jumped to 77.9 from 71.1 in August. That increase suggested that companies are facing higher costs for materials and other inputs, reinforcing concerns that inflation could remain above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/us-manufacturing-steady-september-input-prices-increase-2026-10-01/))

The labor market provided another positive signal for economic activity but also complicated the inflation outlook. Weekly initial jobless claims fell to 197,000, below the 200,000 economists polled by Reuters had expected. The figure pointed to continued resilience in employment conditions just before the release of the September nonfarm payrolls report.

For the Federal Reserve, the data creates a difficult balance. Policymakers need to judge whether inflation is cooling sufficiently while also considering whether economic growth and employment remain strong enough to tolerate restrictive monetary policy. The central bank raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points in September to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first rate increase in three years. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/us-manufacturing-steady-september-input-prices-increase-2026-10-01/))

Fed officials offered somewhat different signals this week. New York Fed President John Williams said there was no need for urgency in changing policy and suggested that one further increase could be appropriate later in the year. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson similarly said officials needed more data before deciding on future adjustments. Those comments sharply reduced market expectations for an October increase. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/fed-may-take-time-make-next-interest-rate-move-jefferson-says-2026-10-01/))

According to Reuters, traders were pricing only about a 25% probability of a rate increase at the October 27-28 meeting on Thursday, compared with roughly 70% earlier in the week. The change followed softer-than-expected August inflation data and the comments from Williams and Jefferson. However, other officials remained more concerned about inflation, showing that the debate inside the central bank is not settled. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/fed-may-take-time-make-next-interest-rate-move-jefferson-says-2026-10-01/))

Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he remained open to another increase, although he did not have a strong view about whether it should happen at the October meeting. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said at least another half percentage point of increases might eventually be needed to bring inflation back toward the Fed's 2% objective. These comments highlight the difference between near-term market expectations and the possibility of additional tightening later in the year. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/fed-may-take-time-make-next-interest-rate-move-jefferson-says-2026-10-01/))

Oil markets added another source of pressure. Brent crude settled more than $4 higher on Thursday after China suspended fuel exports, raising concerns about global supply. Brent finished above $102 a barrel, while the rise in crude prices helped lift the S&P 500 energy sector by 1.9%, making it the strongest-performing major sector of the session.

Higher oil prices are a complicated factor for equities. Energy companies can benefit from rising crude prices because their revenues and profits can increase, but expensive oil can raise transportation, manufacturing and consumer costs elsewhere in the economy. For monetary policymakers, a sustained energy-price increase can make inflation more persistent, potentially extending a period of restrictive interest rates. Reuters reported that rising oil and diesel prices have become increasingly important contributors to the bond-market selloff. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/markets/econ-world/yield-gain-housing-pain-2026-10-01/))

Artificial intelligence offered a counterweight to the macroeconomic pressures. Semiconductor and technology stocks remained relatively resilient, helped by strong corporate investment in AI infrastructure. Micron Technology rose about 3% after delivering a strong revenue forecast, while Nvidia and Applied Materials also gained. The strength of these companies reflects investor expectations that spending on AI data centers, chips and related infrastructure can continue supporting earnings even as financing costs rise. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/global-markets-global-markets-2026-10-01/))

Accenture provided another boost to the technology and information-services sector. The company's shares jumped 22% after it forecast fiscal 2027 revenue growth of 3% to 6%, above the average analyst expectation. The outlook reduced some concerns that AI automation would rapidly disrupt traditional IT-services businesses and helped lift shares of other companies in the sector.

The broader market nevertheless remains uneven. At the end of September, the S&P 500 had reached levels supported by strong technology performance, but a significant portion of individual companies had underperformed. Reuters noted that about 40% of S&P 500 companies were down for the year, illustrating how much of the market's strength has been concentrated in a relatively narrow group of large technology and AI-related stocks. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/commentary/reuters-open-interest/global-markets-q3-roi-column-pix-graphics-2026-10-01/))

That concentration could become increasingly important if Treasury yields remain high. Large technology companies often carry valuations based on expectations of earnings growth far into the future, making them sensitive to changes in interest rates and bond yields. Yet these companies also have unusually strong cash flows and exposure to AI investment, which can help them absorb higher financing costs better than some smaller or more indebted companies.

The first trading day of October therefore delivered a mixed message. Stocks demonstrated resilience by recovering from an early decline, but the gains were small and came only after yields retreated from a multi-decade high. The combination of strong manufacturing demand, low jobless claims and rising input prices also suggests that investors still have to contend with an economy that is growing while inflation remains a concern.

The next major test was already approaching as the session ended: the September employment report. Economists surveyed by Reuters expected nonfarm payrolls to rise by about 90,000 and the unemployment rate to remain at 4.1%. A stronger report could strengthen the case for additional monetary tightening, while weaker hiring could reinforce the argument for a more cautious Federal Reserve. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/us-manufacturing-steady-september-input-prices-increase-2026-10-01/))

Markets will also continue watching oil for signs that the energy shock is either easing or becoming more persistent. Geopolitical tensions involving Iran, disruptions to fuel supplies and changes in Chinese exports have created large swings in crude prices. Any sustained move higher would have implications not only for energy companies but also for inflation expectations, consumer spending and the direction of Treasury yields. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/global-markets-global-markets-2026-10-01/))

For now, Wall Street has entered the fourth quarter on relatively firm footing despite a difficult bond-market environment. The S&P 500 remains about 12% higher for the year, while the Nasdaq is up about 15.6% and the Dow roughly 6%, according to AP. Those gains provide context for the latest volatility: the market is not entering October after a broad collapse, but investors are increasingly sensitive to higher borrowing costs and inflation risks.

The opening session of October ultimately showed why markets may remain volatile through the coming weeks. AI spending and strong corporate results continue to support equities, while Treasury yields near multi-decade highs and oil above $100 a barrel create an opposing force. The Federal Reserve's next moves will depend heavily on incoming inflation and employment data, while investors will simultaneously have to assess whether corporate earnings can keep pace with the cost of capital.
